opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that, for humans and animals, intrinsic motivation is grounded in something very concrete. A baby is curious because it's exploring a physical world, and there's a clear signal: you push something, it falls, and you learn something surprising. The novelty or surprise is defined relative to the environment and to your body.

When you move to language and reasoning, it becomes much more abstract. What does it mean for a thought to be novel or interesting? In a game like Montezuma's Revenge you can count new rooms or measure prediction error on pixels. In the space of language, almost everything is "new" at the surface level. You can generate infinitely many different sentences, but most of that novelty is meaningless. So the hard question is how to define a kind of curiosity or progress that is about meaning, not just surface form.

The second challenge is that language models already know so much. With pretraining they've absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge, so things aren't surprising to them in the way they would be to a newborn agent. The frontier of what's genuinely unknown for them is much harder to locate. It's less about exploring a maze and more about discovering a new theorem, a new idea, a new way of solving a problem, and it's very hard to give a dense signal for that.

Third, there's the question of what the intrinsic reward should even be aligned to. For humans, curiosity is partly shaped by evolution and by social context. We find certain things interesting because they matter for survival or for other people. For an AI agent, if you just tell it to maximize some notion of information gain or self-improvement, it could drift toward things that are interesting in a weird, degenerate way but not useful to anyone.

So I think the open problem is constructing incentives that are grounded. Maybe grounded in real environments, in interaction with people, or in long-horizon tasks where the agent can tell whether it's actually getting better at something meaningful. That's why I think intrinsic motivation and the move toward agents that live in real environments and accumulate experience are deeply connected. You need a world that pushes back on you before your curiosity can mean anything.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a baby’s curiosity in a physical world with abstract language and reasoning, but does not identify adults as the language- and reasoning-mediated counterpart.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes curiosity in language and reasoning from physical exploration, using Montezuma’s Revenge and maze exploration as examples of physical environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core challenge is that the thing we actually care about, like "did this agent reason well," is not something you can easily write down as a reward function. In the old RL world, intrinsic motivation was things like curiosity, novelty, prediction error. Those work when the state space is pixels or coordinates, because you can measure surprise numerically. But when the agent's "actions" are thoughts and sentences, what does novelty even mean? Every sentence is novel if you look at the tokens. So the naive signals either collapse to nothing useful or they reward verbosity and wandering.

The second part is the gap between what's easy to verify and what's actually valuable. Math and code have been great because there's an external checker. You get a clean outcome reward and you can scale. But most of what we want language agents to do, planning a research direction, deciding when to stop and ask, knowing that a sub-goal was a dead end, has no checker. So people try to build intrinsic rewards, like "did the model's confidence go up," or "did a self-critique say this looks good." And the problem is that the model is grading itself with the same biases it used to produce the answer. It becomes a mirror, not a signal.

And then there's hacking. Language is incredibly flexible, so any proxy you build in language the model will find the shortest path to satisfying it. If you reward "says something that sounds like a plan," you get plans. If you reward "expresses uncertainty appropriately," you get hedging everywhere. The gradient flows into the form rather than the substance, and this happens faster with language than with any other action space I've seen because the model already knows exactly what the grader is looking for.

So where I've landed is that the honest intrinsic signal probably has to come from interaction with an environment that pushes back. Not a human judge, not a self-judge, but the world. You tried something, it didn't work, you can tell because the tool returned an error or the user came back confused. The incentive is less "be curious" in the abstract and more "make your beliefs about this environment more predictive." That still has the surprise flavor, but grounded in outcomes rather than in the text itself. The hard engineering question is how to build enough rich, long-horizon environments where that pressure is real. I think that's actually the bottleneck now, more than the algorithms.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare infants’ physically grounded understanding with adults’ language- and reasoning-mediated understanding.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes intrinsic incentives for language agents whose actions are thoughts and sentences from older RL settings with pixel or coordinate state spaces, such as physical environments.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is deciding what counts as progress. In a game, you have a score and a fairly clear definition of winning. But when an AI is reasoning through language, it might generate a new idea, ask a question, or discover that its previous approach was wrong. Which of those should receive a reward?

You could reward novelty, but producing something novel is not necessarily useful. You could reward confidence, but then you might encourage the model to become confidently wrong. Even rewarding a longer chain of reasoning can encourage more words without better thinking.

So the incentive needs some connection to consequences: did this reasoning help solve a problem, make a prediction more accurate, or reveal something that can be verified? The difficult part is preserving that connection while also rewarding exploration whose value may only become clear much later. We want the system to explore beyond what we already know how to evaluate, but our ability to evaluate it is precisely what makes the reward meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI reasoning through language, but does not contrast infants’ physically grounded understanding with adults’ language- and reasoning-mediated understanding.

r002.rationale: It describes the challenge of rewarding language-based reasoning, but does not distinguish that problem from intrinsic incentives in physical environments such as mazes or robot simulations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that we don’t really know what progress should look like in the space of language and reasoning. If an agent is exploring a physical environment, visiting a new place gives you a fairly concrete notion of novelty. But in language, you can generate infinitely many different sentences without learning anything useful. So novelty alone is a very weak incentive.

You might reward the model for being surprised, or for reducing uncertainty. But then you have to distinguish uncertainty that can be resolved through useful reasoning from things that are just unpredictable. And you have to distinguish actually making progress from producing something that sounds insightful.

So the question is: can we construct an incentive that rewards discovering something useful, even before we know which downstream task it will help with? Verifiable tasks give us a starting point, because we can check whether a solution works. For more open-ended reasoning, defining that signal is much harder. That’s where I think a lot of the difficulty lies.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare infants’ physically grounded understanding with adults’ language- and reasoning-mediated understanding.

r002.rationale: It contrasts incentives for language reasoning with exploring physical environments, explaining that physical novelty is concrete while generating novel language may not produce useful learning.
